citations.sentence: Worship leaders have built AI tools that help plan setlists and score songs on qualities like scriptural grounding, Christianity Today reported on Oct 2 [[1]].
One, SongTheology, grades a single song's lyrics. The other, Asaph, tracks the balance of a church's song choices over time [[1]].
Both tools run on Claude, an AI model [[1]].
Worship leader Tyler Anson Newberry wrote the scoring grid. The tool uses Claude to analyze lyrics "pulled from Google" and give theological feedback [[1]].
A song can earn up to 35 points across seven categories, including "scriptural grounding," "gospel presence" and "pastoral durability" [[1]].
Each category is scored 1 to 5. A total of 30 to 35 reads "Use freely," and anything below 18 reads "Probably avoid" [[2]].
God-centeredness asks, "Where is the center of gravity: God’s character and works, or mainly my experience of God?" Pastoral durability asks, "Can someone suffering sing it honestly?" [[2]]

The page says the tool "evaluates lyrics only, irrespective of artist or church affiliation." Leaders can also score their own original lyrics, which the site says are "used only to generate this score, then discarded" [[2]].
Newberry and his wife, Leslianne Newberry, left full-time church ministry just over a year ago to start Asaph's Table, a nonprofit that supports and trains worship leaders [[1]].
"A lot of younger worship leaders don’t have a mental theology grid for the worship songs they encounter," he told CT [[1]].
The most-searched song so far is the hymn "Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing" [[1]].
CT reported that the popular song "Gratitude" by Brandon Lake scores 20 out of 35, with flags for "gospel clarity" and "emotion without theological grounding" [[1]].
It is designed to track "the emotional and theological balance of a church’s worship sets over time" [[1]].
The company says a church can import its song library and see "underused themes, gaps in theology or overused emotions" [[3]].
It can sync with the church-planning service Planning Center through a browser extension, or work from an uploaded spreadsheet [[3]].
Like SongTheology, Asaph relies on Claude [[1]].
"It’s doing a lot of the grunt work, and there is still a human in the loop," he said [[1]].
He was plain about the model's limits, too: "AI is not trained to think about this stuff" [[1]].
The company tells users "you always have final say" [[3]]
and that "Technology can't replace your pastoral heart" [[4]].
Both founders wrote their own evaluation criteria and use Claude to apply them, and neither tool is endorsed by a particular denomination or tradition [[1]].
Christianity Today's report describes no independent evaluation of either tool's scores. The results described here are the tools' own output, as reported by Christianity Today and the companies.
citations.note: Attributed absence (factcheck fix): CT's report is silent on any independent evaluation; checkable against source 1.

citations.sentence: Mark Porter, a researcher of congregational music who has served churches as a worship leader, director of music, organist and choir leader [[5]], tested Asaph for CT.

"It can put together a coherent musical set," he said. "I think anything that pushes people to be more reflective about the selection of music can be a good thing. But there’s the question ‘Does this tool do that?’" [[1]]
He calls SongTheology "a tool to help you begin to not need this tool" [[1]].
The ELCA has released a six-page theological foundation paper on artificial intelligence that, Living Lutheran reports, is not new social teaching but "the beginning of a conversation" [[6]].

The paper asks that "every application of AI includes human beings in the loop who remain accountable for its use," and it names "the potential reduction in human capacity for critical thinking" as a danger [[7]].
Evangelization Lab trains dioceses and parishes to turn their digital presence into "a much more active source of interpersonal communication," OSV News reported Sept 28 [[8]].
The aim is to help seekers move off the internet and "into a space where you are in a sacramental loving relationship with Christ and his Church" [[8]].
Both founders wrote their own criteria, and no denomination stands behind either tool [[1]].
CT notes that the people using AI to build these tools "also have a point of view that informs the instructions they are giving the technology" [[1]].
"Over time, they acquire meanings and uses that aren’t captured in the text," he said [[1]].
"You can’t use it to shortcut your own reflection and engagement," Porter said [[1]].

Writing in Reformed Worship in July, Benjamin P. Snoek drew the line in the same place: "There is a problem, though, when we leverage technology to shortcut, not support, the priestly work incumbent on worship leaders" [[9]].
